\section[iūrgium, iūrgiī]{iūrgium, iūrgiī — a quarrel, dispute}

\label{lesson:LA-C537-iurgium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a darling, then the Latin for a gift.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: iūrgium, iūrgiī}
\textbf{iūrgium, iūrgiī} — \textquotedblleft{}a quarrel, dispute\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Inter frātrēs saepe iūrgium est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is often a quarrel between the brothers.}
\end{quote}

Neuter, second declension. A quarrel of words, at home or between neighbours.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{iūrgium} is built on \emph{iūrgō} \textquotedblleft{}to quarrel\textquotedblright{}, which Lewis \& Short takes from \emph{iūs} \textquotedblleft{}right, law\textquotedblright{} and \emph{agō} \textquotedblleft{}to drive\textquotedblright{}; EtymDB agrees on \emph{iūs}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iūrgium, iūrgiī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iūrgium, iūrgiī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{iūrgium, iūrgiī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a darling, then the Latin for a gift, then say \emph{iūrgium, iūrgiī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does iūrgium, iūrgiī mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A quarrel, dispute\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[reconciliō, reconciliāre]{reconciliō, reconciliāre — to reconcile, bring together again}

\label{lesson:LA-C537-reconcilio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a gift, then the Latin for a quarrel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: reconciliō, reconciliāre}
\textbf{reconciliō, reconciliāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to reconcile, bring together again\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Māter frātrēs post iūrgium reconciliat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Mother reconciles the brothers after the quarrel.}
\end{quote}

\emph{reconciliō, reconciliāre, reconciliāvī, reconciliātum}: \emph{re-} 'again' + \emph{conciliō} 'to bring together'. English \emph{reconcile}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{reconciliō} is built on \emph{re-} \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \emph{conciliō} \textquotedblleft{}to bring together\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{concilium} \textquotedblleft{}a gathering\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short). English \emph{reconcile} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{reconciliō, reconciliāre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a gift, then the Latin for a quarrel, then say \emph{reconciliō, reconciliāre} again
\end{itemize}

\section[dōnō, dōnāre]{dōnō, dōnāre — to give as a present}

\label{lesson:LA-C537-dono}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a quarrel, then the Latin for to reconcile.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dōnō, dōnāre}
\textbf{dōnō, dōnāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to give as a present\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Avus nepōtī librum dōnat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Grandfather gives his grandson a book as a present.}
\end{quote}

\emph{dōnō, dōnāre, dōnāvī, dōnātum}: \emph{alicui aliquid dōnāre}, or \emph{aliquem aliquā rē dōnāre}. English \emph{donate}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dōnō} is built on \emph{dōnum} \textquotedblleft{}a gift\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short). English \emph{donate} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[īnfīdus, īnfīda, īnfīdum]{īnfīdus, īnfīda, īnfīdum — faithless, untrustworthy}

\label{lesson:LA-C537-infidus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to reconcile, then the Latin for to give as a present.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: īnfīdus, īnfīda, īnfīdum}
\textbf{īnfīdus, īnfīda, īnfīdum} — \textquotedblleft{}faithless, untrustworthy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Amīcus īnfīdus omnia, quae dīxī, aliīs nārrat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The faithless friend tells others everything I said.}
\end{quote}

\emph{in-} 'not' + \emph{fīdus} 'faithful'.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{īnfīdus} is built on \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{fīdus} \textquotedblleft{}faithful\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{fīdō} \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[dēserō, dēserere]{dēserō, dēserere — to abandon, desert}

\label{lesson:LA-C537-desero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to give as a present, then the Latin for faithless.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēserō, dēserere}
\textbf{dēserō, dēserere} — \textquotedblleft{}to abandon, desert\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Amīcus vērus amīcum in perīculō nōn dēserit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A true friend does not abandon his friend in danger.}
\end{quote}

\emph{dēserō, dēserere, dēseruī, dēsertum}: \emph{dē-} 'away' + \emph{serō} 'to join' — to break a tie. English \emph{desert}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dēserō} is built on \emph{dē-} \textquotedblleft{}away\textquotedblright{} and \emph{serō} \textquotedblleft{}to join, link\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to break off a tie. English \emph{desert} comes from its participle \emph{dēsertus}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
